title: Creational Design Patterns Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision of the five classic creational patterns: Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder and Prototype. Covers intent, structure, when to use each, and the pitfalls to avoid.

chapters.title: Creational Patterns: The Mental Model
points: Creational patterns decouple what gets created from the code that asks for it, so callers depend on an interface, not a concrete class

The five patterns: Singleton (one instance), Factory Method (subclass picks the type), Abstract Factory (families of related objects), Builder (step-by-step construction), Prototype (clone an existing object)
Core question each answers: Singleton = how many? Factory Method = which class? Abstract Factory = which family? Builder = how to assemble? Prototype = copy from what?
Smell that signals a need: scattered `new ConcreteClass()` calls, constructors with many parameters, or switch statements on a type tag
Rule of thumb: start with a plain constructor and refactor to a pattern only when the variation actually appears

chapters.title: Singleton and Factory Method
points: Singleton intent: guarantee exactly one instance with a global access point; structure is a private constructor, a static field and a static getInstance()
Thread safety: lazy init needs a lock or double-checked locking with a volatile field; an eager static initializer or an enum singleton is safe by default

Singleton pitfalls: hidden global state, hard to unit test (cannot swap in a mock), and it breaks when you need one per tenant or per process; prefer dependency injection with a single shared instance
Factory Method intent: a base class declares create(), and subclasses decide which concrete product to return; the creator calls create() inside its own logic

Use Factory Method when the exact class is unknown until runtime or a framework must let users plug in their own product type; pitfall: a subclass per product explodes the class count, so use a simple static factory if you do not need extension

chapters.title: Abstract Factory and Builder
points: Abstract Factory intent: an interface with one create method per product in a family (e.g. createButton() and createCheckbox()), and each concrete factory returns a matching set (DarkThemeFactory, LightThemeFactory)
Use Abstract Factory when products must be used together and never mixed across families, such as UI themes or cross-platform widgets or per-database DAOs
Abstract Factory pitfall: adding a new product type means changing the interface and every concrete factory; it is easy to add families but costly to add products
Builder intent: separate construction of a complex object from its representation; chained calls like new Pizza.Builder().size(L).cheese().build() produce an immutable result
Builder pitfalls: build() must validate required fields, and a Builder is overkill for objects with two or three fields; use it for many optional parameters (the telescoping constructor problem)

chapters.title: Prototype and Choosing Between Patterns
points: Prototype intent: create new objects by cloning an existing instance via a clone() method, which avoids costly initialization such as DB loads or heavy configuration
Prototype pitfall: shallow copy shares nested references so mutating the clone changes the original; implement a deep copy for mutable nested fields, and watch for circular references
Factory Method vs Abstract Factory: one product vs a family of products; Factory Method uses inheritance, Abstract Factory uses composition of an object
Builder vs Factory: a Factory returns the finished object in one call, while a Builder assembles it in steps and lets you vary the parts; Abstract Factory can use Builders or Prototypes internally

Pick quickly: need exactly one = Singleton, many optional params = Builder, unknown class at runtime = Factory Method, matched families = Abstract Factory, object costly to create but cheap to copy = Prototype

chapters.title: Common Mistakes with Creational Patterns
points: Using Singleton as a convenient global: it hides dependencies and makes tests order-dependent; inject the instance instead
Lazy Singleton without synchronization: two threads can both create an instance under concurrent first access
Applying a Factory or Builder to a simple object: extra indirection with no variation to justify it (over-engineering)
Returning a shallow Prototype clone of an object that holds mutable collections, causing shared-state bugs
Builder without validation in build(): you get half-constructed objects that fail later, far from the cause

chapters.title: Creational Patterns Cheat Sheet
points: Singleton: one instance, private constructor + static getInstance(); use an enum or eager init for thread safety; inject rather than reach for it globally
Factory Method: subclass overrides create() to return one product; use when the class is unknown until runtime
Abstract Factory: one interface producing a family of related products; easy to add families, hard to add products
Builder: stepwise construction with a final build() that validates; use for many optional parameters, result is often immutable
Prototype: clone() an existing object; always decide between a shallow and a deep copy before using it
